[
1
]

Dr. Inderjit Singh Chohan
appeals the dismissal of his defamation action against the respondents. If
successful, Dr. Chohan also challenges the trial judge’s assessment of damages and his disposition as to
costs.

THE PARTIES

[
2
]

Dr. Chohan is a respected
forensic psychiatrist who holds positions at Forensic Assessment and Community
Services (“FACS”), the outpatient unit of the Alberta Hospital
Edmonton and the Royal Alexandra Hospital. He began working at the Forensic
Unit of the Alberta Hospital Edmonton in 1997, dividing his time between the
inpatient unit and FACS. In 2000, he ceased providing services at the inpatient
facility and started working full-time in FACS. In 2001, he started dividing
his practice between FACS and the Royal Alexandra Hospital, a position which
continued throughout the relevant period. In December 2004, Chohan was promoted
from Clinical Lecturer to Assistant Clinical Professor.

[
3
]

Dr. Otakar Cadsky is now retired. Before retiring, he was a respected forensic
psychiatrist at FACS, and generally credited with establishing the FACS unit
and overseeing its growth from one full-time and one part-time psychiatrist to
a facility with 13 full and part-time psychiatrists at the time of trial. Dr.
Cadsky held the position of clinical coordinator until 2001, and from March 31,
2003 until he retired in 2006. Although he was relieved of the position in 2001
as a disciplinary measure for a racist remark he made about another
psychiatrist, in a private conversation (referring to him as a “greedy Jew”, or
words to that effect), he continued to perform many of the duties of clinical
coordinator until his reinstatement on March 31, 2003. That reinstatement was
part of a settlement that concluded the legal proceeding he commenced following
the disciplinary measure. Dr. Cadsky reported to Dr. John Brooks, Clinical
Director of Forensic Psychiatry at the Alberta Hospital until late 2003 when
Dr. Brooks retired.

[
4
]

The Alberta Hospital Edmonton first operated under the Alberta Mental
Health Board, but transferred to the Capital Health Authority on April 1, 2003.
At all relevant times, Dr. Kenneth Gardener was the Chief Medical Officer and
Vice President of Capital Health. The defamation alleged against him regards a
statement he made to Dr. Norman Block, the head of the Psychiatric Unit at the
Royal Alexandra Hospital. Capital Health is sued as the employer of Dr.
Gardener.

[
5
]

At all relevant times, Dr. Rose Dempsey held the position of Acting
Medical Director or Medical Director of the Alberta Hospital Edmonton. She
assumed responsibility as the Clinical Director of Forensic Psychiatry after
Dr. Brooks retired. Dr. Dempsey took a sabbatical leave in September 2004,
returning in October 2005. She now limits herself to clinical work and refuses
to

be involved in
administration. Dr. Friend was appointed to fill Dr. Dempsey’s position in
September 2004.

[
6
]

Dr. Glen Baker was the Chair of the University of Alberta Department of
Psychiatry. He holds a Ph.D. in Biological Psychiatry. He headed a project
involving the establishment of an Academic Forensic Unit at the University. In
that context, he met with all FACS psychiatrists, including Dr. Chohan.
Following a meeting with Dr. Chohan, Dr. Baker phoned Drs. Block and Gardener
expressing concerns about Dr. Chohan’s health.

[
7
]

Dr. Larry Ohlhauser, the former Registrar of the College of Physicians
and Surgeons, had some expertise in resolving issues faced by physicians. He
had a special interest in mental health issues. Dr. Ohlhauser initially became
involved at the request of Dr. Gordon King, a psychiatrist at FACS and friend
of Dr. Chohan, who was concerned about Dr. Chohan’s reaction to the lack of
action on his complaints of harassment and intimidation. Following a meeting
with Dr. Chohan, Dr. Ohlhauser phoned Dr. Gardener to express his concerns
about Dr. Chohan’s health.

FACTS

[
8
]

One of Dr. Chohan’s claims relates to a statement made by Dr.
Cadsky. Specifically, Dr. Cadsky referred to Dr. Chohan as a “paranoid Sikh” in
a conversation with Dr. Santoch Singh Rai and Dr. Curtis Woods. Dr. Chohan also
claims that the other defendants, Drs. Ohlhauser, Baker, and Gardener, made
statements that defamed him when he sought redress for Dr. Cadsky’s statement
and his complaints of harassment and intimidation
in the working environment at FACS.

[
9
]

Both Drs. Rai and Woods were psychiatrists at FACS, and had visited the
Cadsky home in early February 2003. At the time, and since early November 2002,
Dr. Cadsky was on a leave of absence for personal and health reasons. His
daughter had been diagnosed with Hodgkins Disease in 2001, and died in December
of 2002. He had taken a leave of absence to be with his daughter in the latter
part of her illness. Two weeks after her death in early December 2002, Dr.
Cadsky suffered a myocardial infarction and had a quintuple bypass. In
addition, his marriage was in the process of breakdown.

[
10
]

While there was a social component to the visit, the three psychiatrists
soon turned their discussion to work-related issues. Some administrative
changes had been proposed by the FACS Manager during Dr. Cadsky’s absence and
Dr. Rai wanted to discuss these with Dr. Cadsky. They retired to the family
room area of the Cadsky’s residence, where he offered his visitors a glass of
wine. Dr. Cadsky listened to Dr. Rai’s explanation of the proposed initiatives,
and assured his visitors that the initiatives would not be adopted. Dr. Cadsky
testified that the discussion then turned to the anticipated resignation of Dr.
Brooks. Dr. Cadsky says that the others were interested in his view on who
should be appointed as the new Clinical Director. Accordingly, he opined on whether
other psychiatrists working at FACS might replace Dr. Brooks. He gave terse,
two-worded

descriptions of the various
psychiatrists reflecting his views of each candidate. For instance, he referred
to certain individuals as being a “disorganized Mexican,” a “narcissistic
Spaniard,” and an “English diva.” Dr. Cadsky admits that he referred to Dr.
Chohan as a “paranoid Sikh.” Drs. Rai and Woods testified that Dr. Cadsky
called Dr. Chohan a “paranoid Sikh” and expressed an intent to provoke a fight
with Dr. Chohan as a means of forcing him to resign. Dr. Cadsky denied
expressing any such intention, but conceded that he may have stated that Dr.
Chohan had a propensity for “getting into snits and walking out” and speculated
that this would occur again at FACS. Neither Dr. Woods nor Dr. Rai were able to
recall additional context of the conversation or the circumstances that led to
the comment. Although neither Drs. Rai or Woods objected to Dr. Cadsky’s
language, they both considered his remarks to be offensive and inappropriate.

[
11
]

Both Drs. Rai and Woods recalled Dr. Cadsky advising them when they
first started working at FACS that Dr.Chohan was known to be quick to anger and
advised them to stay away from him.

[
12
]

Dr. Cadsky testified that he considered the conversation to be
private, with no expectation that his comments would be repeated. He indicated
that his use of the term “Sikh” was merely intended to describe Dr. Chohan’s
appearance. Dr. Chohan is a proud and devout practitioner of the Sikh religion.
Dr. Cadsky also expressed his professional view that Dr. Chohan met the
clinical diagnosis for a paranoid personality disorder, as he exhibited four of
seven characteristics typically associated with that disorder. Dr. Cadsky
explained that, generally, he based this opinion on what he had been told of
Dr. Chohan’s confrontations with others. Dr. Cadsky also testified that he
always considered Dr. Chohan to be a good psychiatrist and that the personality
issues did not affect his ability as a psychiatrist. He explained at trial that
he was not intending to be malicious in describing any of the psychiatrists and
thought that he had a good relationship with most of the other psychiatrists he
discussed. He also stated that he respected
Dr. Chohan’s ability as a psychiatrist
and believed his work to be of high quality.

[
13
]

Although not cordial, the relationship between Drs. Cadsky and Chohan
was respectful and professional throughout the period prior to March 31, 2003.
Dr. Chohan testified that Dr. Cadsky was always nice to him and that there had
been no difficulty between them. Dr. Cadsky testified that he always treated
Dr. Chohan respectfully but carefully, as he had a reputation for being quick
tempered and walking out when things did not go his way. Dr. Cadsky referred to
the events surrounding Dr. Chohan’s leaving the forensic inpatient service unit
and moving full-time to FACS in 2000, and an incident involving Dr. Bland. No
other witness pointed to any conflict between them, and there is no suggestion
in the evidence that Dr. Cadsky subsequently tried to instigate any argument
with Dr. Chohan.

[
14
]

Dr. Cadsky returned to work at FACS in March, initially on a part-time
basis, and on a full-time basis by the end of the month. On March 31, 2003, Dr.
Cadsky was reinstated as the clinical coordinator at FACS following the
settlement of the action he commenced after being demoted for referring to
another psychiatrist as a “greedy Jew.” Dr. Cadsky’s reinstatement occurred on
the eve of the transfer of the Alberta Hospital Edmonton from the Mental Health
Board to the Capital Health Authority effective April 1, 2003.

[
15
]

In 2001, after Dr. Cadsky’s demotion, a group of FACS
psychiatrists, including Dr. Chohan, wrote a letter to Dr. Beausejour, then
Acting Medical Director of Alberta Hospital Edmonton. While they were not condoning Cadsky’s comment about the other psychiatrist, they expressed their view that
the complaint had not been dealt with appropriately and requested that Dr.
Beausejour review the action he had taken. Dr. Margaret Tweddle, who first
proposed sending the letter, explained that she believed that the Medical
Director had no authority to dismiss Dr. Cadsky from the position of clinical
coordinator, as that could only be done on the recommendation of the Medical
Credentials Committee.

[
16
]

Although Dr. Rai initially said nothing to Dr. Chohan about Dr. Cadsky’s
statement, he became concerned when he learned that Dr. Cadsky had been
reinstated. His concern was that Dr. Cadsky would provoke an argument with Dr.
Chohan and force him to resign from FACS. Accordingly, Dr. Rai advised Dr.
Chohan that Dr. Cadsky had referred to him as a “paranoid Sikh” and planned to
provoke an argument with him so that he would leave FACS. Dr. Chohan confirmed
this conversation with Dr. Woods. Both also told Dr. Chohan that Dr. Cadsky had
earlier told them to stay away from Dr. Chohan as he had a reputation for
irritability. Dr. Rai, who commenced working at FACS some six months earlier,
stated that he was concerned about his special licence to practise in Alberta
and asked Dr. Chohan to keep the information regarding his disclosure of Dr.
Cadsky’s comment confidential.

[
17
]

FACS had not been a happy work place for some time. A number of
issues had arisen, many related to the perceived leadership skills, or lack of
them, of Drs. Brooks and Cadsky and the perceived lack of interest in adopting
new ideas. Dr. Cadsky testified that there appeared to be no overt concerns
about leadership prior to the commencement of his leave, but that the situation
had changed considerably during his absence and following his return. During that time, the more recently appointed
psychiatrists (Drs. Metelitsa, Chohan, King, Demas, Santana, Woods and Rai)
developed dissatisfaction with the stagnation in FACS and the management’s perceived opposition to new ideas. They complained
in general terms of harassment and intimidation, without detailing specific
instances. A theory had developed that psychiatrists who had graduated from
Canadian universities were being discriminated against in favour of foreign
psychiatrists, who would have limited licences and therefore be easier to
control. Dr. Cadsky’s reinstatement
became another source of discontent.

[
18
]

Rumours circulated about Dr.
Brooks’ retirement and the possibility
that Dr. Tweddle, considered to be a member of the “old guard,”
might be appointed to take his place. The seven psychiatrists opposed the
current leadership at FACS, and they met frequently to discuss issues that
concerned them, often in the office of Dr. Metelitsa. Dr. Cadsky testified that
the meetings of the group were disruptive and at times, resulted in patients
being kept waiting for long periods, necessitating reminders by staff or
himself to the psychiatrists.

[
19
]

On April 27, 2003, less than one month after Dr. Cadsky’s reinstatement,
the seven FACS psychiatrists arranged to meet with Dr. Gardener to express
their concerns. In doing so, they bypassed everyone at the Alberta Hospital
Edmonton, including Dr. Cadsky, Dr. Brooks, Dr. Dempsey (Acting Medical
Director of the Alberta Hospital Edmonton) and Dr. Asad Brahim (Brahim), the
President of the Staff Medical Association. The rationale was that these
individuals had supported Dr. Cadsky’s reinstatement. At their meeting with Dr.
Gardener, they complained about Dr. Cadsky’s remark that had led to his
demotion, and opposed his reinstatement on that ground (even though some of
them had signed the letter supporting him in 2001). They raised a number of
complaints, all of a general nature regarding intimidation, harassment, hiring
practices and lack of acceptance of new ideas and programs. Although Dr. Chohan
had advised most, if not all, of the group about Dr. Cadsky’s “paranoid Sikh”
comment, no one mentioned it, or his threat to force Dr. Chohan to resign.

[
20
]

In May 27, 2003, Dr. Gardener, Eleanor Grant (Chief Operating Officer,
Capital Health) and Dr. Dempsey met with the forensic medical staff. Dr.
Dempsey chaired the meeting. While some were concerned that a meeting involving
all FACS psychiatrists would inhibit discussion, that obviously did not occur.
That meeting provided an opportunity for all psychiatrists to air their
concerns, and gave Dr. Gardener an opportunity to outline the process to deal
with the complaints. Dr. Chohan testified that the meeting commenced with a
discussion of transitional administrative issues. He interrupted that
discussion after 15 minutes and indicated that the issues raised in the April
meeting with Dr. Gardener should be discussed. Dr. Chohan expressed his
objections to Dr. Cadsky’s reinstatement on the basis of the racist comment he
had made in 2001, essentially demanding that the reinstatement be revoked.
There was discussion about leadership problems at FACS, including intimidation
and harassment by Drs. Cadsky and Brooks, both of whom were present at the
meeting. Dr. Chohan’s position was openly supported by Drs. Rai and Woods, as
well as others. Again, no one mentioned Dr. Cadsky’s “paranoid Sikh” comment or
his threat to provoke an argument with Dr. Chohan, either at that meeting or
immediately following to either Dr. Dempsey or Dr. Gardener.

[
21
]

Dr. Chohan testified that he did not mention the “paranoid Sikh” comment
or the threat to force him to resign at the meeting because Dr. Rai had
repeated his request that he treat the disclosure as confidential. Dr. Rai
stated that he did not wish to have his disclosure of the conversation
discussed in an open meeting as he was concerned about his temporary licence to
practise in Alberta. Considering that Dr. Rai openly opposed Dr. Cadsky’s
reinstatement in the meeting, it is difficult to understand why he continued to
insist that his disclosure of Dr. Cadsky’s “paranoid Sikh” comment remain
private.

[
22
]

At the meeting, Dr. Gardener advised that all future complaints were to
be first referred to Dr. Dempsey. Dr. Gardener testified that he had already
privately decided that the leadership of Dr. Brooks was problematic, and left
with Dr. Dempsey the task of persuading Dr. Brooks to resign soon. That
occurred later in the year.

[
23
]

Following the meeting, Dr. Chohan asked to meet alone with Dr. Gardener
to discuss these issues. Having just established a procedure whereby complaints
were to go to Dr. Dempsey, Dr. Gardener refused to meet without Dr. Dempsey,
stating that he would not bypass Dr. Dempsey and the system that had just been
set up to deal with complaints.

[
24
]

The evidence differed as to whether this meeting, in fact, took place.
Dr. Gardener’s assistant initially set up a meeting in his diary for Dr.
Dempsey and Dr Chohan on June 3, 2003, and Dr. Chohan acknowledged that Dr.
Gardener at first refused to see him without Dr. Dempsey. Dr. Chohan testified
that Dr. Gardener later changed his mind, that he and Dr. Gardener met alone on
June 3, and that he told Dr. Gardener about Dr. Cadsky’s “paranoid Sikh”
comment and his threat to force Dr. Chohan to resign. Dr. Chohan testified that
Dr. Gardener did not appear to be interested in listening to these complaints
and urged him to forget about them and move on.

[
25
]

Dr. Gardener does not recall meeting with Dr. Chohan on June 3rd, and
denied knowing about the “paranoid Sikh” comment until March 2004, several
months later. He also denied telling Dr. Chohan to move on.

[
26
]

Dr. Chohan also relies on a letter he sent to Dr. Gardener dated August
22, 2003, where he refers to a meeting between him and Dr. Gardener on June 3,
2003. In that letter, Dr. Chohan listed the concerns raised in the April 27
meeting, as follows:

(a.) Concerns arising with respect
to your appointment or approval of a certain appointment;

(b) Concerns respecting
intimidation in the workplace;

(c) Concerns respecting
exclusionary practices;

(d) concerns respecting selective
hiring practices.

[
27
]

In reference to the purported meeting on June 3 with Dr. Gardener, Dr.
Chohan further stated:

Again the concerns in the workplace
were reviewed and discussed.

Furthermore we had discussed the
concern that as a result of certain workplace practices; it appeared that
Canadian Graduates might well have been discouraged from placing applications
for positions. ...

Dr. Chohan also mentioned his
concern that federal immigration laws and regulations were not being properly
followed.

[
28
]

Although the letter was a private communication to Dr. Gardener, Dr.
Chohan made no mention, even indirectly, of Dr. Cadsky’s “paranoid Sikh”
comment or the purported threat to force him to resign, or of any discussion in
that regard either in the June 3 meeting or otherwise.

[
29
]

Dr. Dempsey testified that she was aware that Dr. Gardener and she were
to meet with Dr. Chohan on June 3, 2003, but that the meeting had been
cancelled because Dr. Chohan refused to meet when she was present. She
testified that Dr. Gardener never informed her that he had met with Dr. Chohan,
and her understanding was that Dr. Gardener would keep her informed of any
developments regarding FACS.

[
30
]

Based on this evidence, the trial judge found that the June 3
rd

meeting did not take place and that Dr. Gardener was not specifically made
aware of the “paranoid Sikh” comment until March 2004.

[
31
]

In June 2003, Dr. King, one of the “group of seven” psychiatrists and an
admirer and friend of Dr. Chohan, became concerned about Dr. Chohan. He felt
that Dr. Chohan might be damaging his career with his continued pursuit of
complaints and that he was making a name for himself as a troublemaker. Dr.
King testified that he and Dr. Metelitsa offered their support and tried to
convince Dr. Chohan to follow other paths, but were unsuccessful in doing so.
Dr. King testified that Dr. Chohan said that he would continue to pursue the
complaints to the end, no matter the cost. Dr. King stated: “I think both of us
felt and said that it was occupying far too much of his time and attention and
wrecking his life. ... [Dr. Chohan] was very angry and outraged.”

[
32
]

On June 13, 2003, Dr. King tried to
discuss his concerns with Dr. Gardener, but he was away. Instead, Dr. King
spoke to Eleanor Grant and told her that he was concerned that Dr. Chohan was
very upset and feeling vulnerable. He suggested that some reassurance would be
in order. Ms. Grant contacted Dr. Dempsey and advised her of the discussion
with Dr. King. Dr. Dempsey testified that in light of Dr. Gardener’s absence, she informed Dr. White, Chief of
Psychiatry, of the information she received regarding Dr. King’s concerns. She also contacted Dr. Baker, who
undertook to contact Dr. Chohan. By this time, Dr. Dempsey was aware that Dr.
Chohan refused to speak to her or attend any meeting where she was present.

[
33
]

Dr. King testified that he spoke to Dr. Dempsey the next day, and
received the impression that she did not know what to do and wanted the issue
buried. Dr. King also expressed his concerns to Dr. Baker. Dr Baker did not
recall any conversation with Dr. Dempsey regarding any concerns about Dr.
Chohan, but recalled discussing general problems at FACS with Dr. King.

[
34
]

Dr. King testified that after discussing his concerns with Dr.
Metelitsa and obtaining his concurrence, he
approached Dr. Ohlhauser, a former Registrar of the College of Physicians and
Surgeons of Alberta, on June 14, 2003. Dr. Ohlhauser was a “father figure”
who had considerable experience working with doctors undergoing problems in
their personal and professional lives. Dr. King initially approached Dr.
Ohlhauser at his office to advise of the concern for Dr. Chohan. Dr. Ohlhauser
was hesitant to get involved, stating that he no longer did that work. Dr. King
persisted, telling Dr. Ohlhauser that Dr. Chohan was angry, frustrated, and
paranoid. While Dr. King’s evidence
denied advising Dr. Ohlhauser that he was using the term “paranoid” in
any clinical sense, Dr. Ohlhauser testified that he confirmed with Dr. King
that he was describing clinical paranoia.

[
35
]

Dr. Ohlhauser also testified that he subsequently met with Dr. Metelitsa
and confirmed that Dr. Metelitsa shared Dr. King’s concerns. At trial, Dr.
Metelitsa denied that this meeting occurred, or that he had or confirmed any
concerns about Dr. Chohan.

[
36
]

Dr. Ohlhauser again met with Dr. King and advised that he was prepared
to meet with Dr. Chohan. He asked Dr. King to recommend another a physician who
could provide support for Dr. Chohan, if needed. Dr. King suggested Dr.
Hibbard, a psychiatrist who worked with Dr. Chohan at the Royal Alexandra
Hospital. Dr. King then advised Dr. Chohan that Dr. Ohlhauser was willing to
meet with him and may be able to help him.

[
37
]

Dr. Chohan arranged a meeting with Dr. Ohlhauser on June 27, 2003. Before the scheduled meeting, Dr.
Ohlhauser attempted to contact Dr. Hibbard, but was unable to do so. He spoke
to Dr. Hibbard’s assistant. Without
specifically identifying Dr. Chohan, Dr. Ohlhauser left a message stating “[w]e have (or may have) a sick doc here, can you
call me?” Dr. Ohlhauser met with Dr.
Chohan. Based on his observations from that meeting, Dr. Ohlhauser became
concerned that there may be a problem. He testified that he thought that Dr.
Chohan was “fixated” on the workplace issues and unable to move beyond
them. Dr. Ohlhauser testified that he learned of the “paranoid Sikh”
comment at this meeting.

[
38
]

Although not a psychiatrist, Dr. Ohlhauser believed that Dr.
Chohan should be assessed. He again attempted to contact Dr. Hibbard, but was
only able to get through to his private voice mail. Dr. Ohlhauser left a
message, stating that Dr. Chohan may be paranoid and inquired whether Dr.
Hibbard would be able to help out. Dr. Hibbard did not check his voice mail
until the following week. Dr. Hibbard testified that
he made no note of the content of the voice mail message and destroyed the
earlier message that had been left by his assistant.

[
39
]

After a brief telephone discussion on June 13, 2003, Drs. Baker and
Chohan agreed to meet on June 25, 2003. Dr. Baker’s primary purpose for the
meeting was to discuss his current project, the creation of an Academic
Forensic Unit at the University of Alberta. In doing so, Dr. Baker was
consulting with all of the forensic psychiatrists at FACS to get their ideas
regarding the project.

[
40
]

Dr. Baker does not recall speaking to Dr. Dempsey prior to the
appointment. He had some general knowledge, largely gleaned from his friends,
Drs. King and Metelitsa, that there was some dissension among the psychiatrists
at FACS. Dr. Baker testified that little time was spent discussing the Academic
Unit project, as Dr. Chohan wanted to discuss the workplace issues at FACS and
his dissatisfaction with the lack of progress on the part of administration in
dealing with his concerns. Dr. Baker testified that Dr. Chohan kept returning
to that topic, and that he was very angry and upset. Based on this discussion,
Dr. Baker became concerned for Dr. Chohan’s well-being.

[
41
]

Dr. Baker phoned Dr. Block, the head of Psychiatric Services at the
Royal Alexandra Hospital, and advised that he thought there may be a problem
with Dr. Chohan. Dr. Block advised

that there was no problem. Dr.
Baker also called Dr. Gardener to advise of his concerns and said that Dr.
Block had assured him that Dr. Chohan was fine.

[
42
]

Dr. Baker denied using the term “paranoid” or “paranoia” in these
conversations, as he was not a psychiatrist, and his experience had taught him
not to stray into psychiatric terminology. He admitted discussing Dr. Chohan’s
state of anger and frustration.

[
43
]

Some time after meeting with Dr. Chohan, Dr. Baker also phoned Dr.
Ohlhauser, as he had encouraged Dr. Chohan to meet with Dr. Ohlhauser and
wanted to know his objective feedback on Dr. Chohan’s condition. Dr. Ohlhauser
agreed with Dr. Baker that Dr. Chohan was quite upset, fixated on the FACS
problems, and unwilling to move on.

[
44
]

On July 3, Dr. Hibbard checked his voice mail and listened to Dr.
Ohlhauser’s message. Since he was acting head of the department in the absence
of Dr. Block, Dr. Hibbard decided to approach Dr. Chohan to find out how he was
doing. In the course of that conversation, Dr. Hibbard advised Dr. Chohan that
he had been contacted by Dr. Ohlhauser, and told him what Dr. Ohlhauser had
said. Dr. Hibbard knew that Dr. Chohan had been stressed about the situation at
FACS, but Dr. Hibbard had previously indicated that he did not wish to discuss
it. After speaking to Dr. Chohan, Dr. Hibbard had no concerns about Dr.
Chohan’s mental state but told him that he was willing to provide assistance if
needed. Dr. Chohan was angry upon learning of Dr. Ohlhauser’s actions. In the
course of their discussion, they were joined by Dr. Block. Drs. Block and
Hibbard talked further after their discussion with Dr. Chohan, and they agreed
that Dr. Chohan was not paranoid and certainly not posing any danger.

[
45
]

Dr. Chohan was understandably shocked and hurt by these developments. He
described the day as the worst day of his life. After this conversation, Dr.
Chohan says that he decided to remain quiet and stopped attending FACS Medical
Staff meetings.

[
46
]

On July 3, 2003, Dr. Ohlhauser,
having received no response from Dr. Hibbard, called Dr. Gardener and advised
that he had met with Dr. Chohan and was concerned that Dr. Chohan may be ill
and may need to be assessed. Dr. Ohlhauser trusted that Dr. Gardener would
manage the problem, if any, from that point.

[
47
]

Dr. Gardener then advised Dr. Block that he had been contacted by two
individuals expressing concern about Dr. Chohan’s mental health, and inquired
whether Dr. Block had noticed any problems. Dr. Block replied that he had no
concerns, but that he would continue to monitor the situation. Dr. Gardener was
satisfied with this response and he left it to Dr. Block to deal with as he saw
fit. Dr. Block testified that to the best of his recollection, both Drs. Baker
and Gardener used the term “paranoid” and stated that the wording of his letter
to Dr. Chohan dated May 14, 2004 accurately reflected his recollection
regarding the statements made by Drs. Baker and Gardener as expressing concerns
“that you may be paranoid.”

[
48
]

The situation at FACS deteriorated in the ensuing months. General complaints of harassment and intimidation
in the workplace and the lack of any action on those complaints, continued.
There were some complaints regarding specific incidents involving Dr. Cadsky,
as well as against Dr. Tweddle and other psychiatrists not party to this
action. The staff meetings degenerated into disputes about minutes and
challenges to decisions. Interruptions and shouting with accusations and
counter accusations became the norm. Indeed, on July 29, Dr. Friend, a
psychiatrist at FACS, wrote to Dr. Brooks to complain that the meetings had
degenerated in shouting matches and name calling, and stated that he was
shocked at the behaviour of his colleagues. He asked Dr. Brooks to enforce some
rules of order in the meetings.

[
49
]

As mentioned earlier, Dr. Chohan sent a letter to Dr. Gardener dated Aug 22, 2003, where he referred to
workplace concerns that had been identified as early as the April 29 meeting.

LAW

Defamation Defined

[
88
]

It is common ground that the correct definition of a defamatory
statement is as set out in Brown at 1-31:

A publication is considered
defamatory if it has the tendency to lower that reputation in the estimation of
reasonable persons in the community.

In order to recover in an action
for defamation, the plaintiff must show:

(1) That the words about which the
plaintiff complains are defamatory;

(2) That they referred to the
plaintiff; and

(3) That they were published to a
third person. [footnotes omitted]

[
89
]

A similar definition is found in the Supreme Court decision
Botiuk
v. Toronto Free Press Publications Ltd.
,
1995 CanLII 60 (SCC)
, [1995] 3 S.C.R. 3 at para.
62
,
126 D.L.R. (4th) 609:

For the purposes of these reasons,
it is sufficient to observe that a publication which tends to lower a person in
the estimation of right‑thinking members of society, or to expose a
person to hatred, contempt or ridicule, is defamatory and will attract
liability. See
Cherneskey v. Armadale Publishers Ltd.
,
1978 CanLII 20 (SCC)
, [1979] 1
S.C.R. 1067, at p. 1079. What is defamatory may be determined from the ordinary
meaning of the published words themselves or from the surrounding
circumstances. In
The Law of Defamation in Canada
(2nd ed. 1994), R. E.
Brown stated the following at p. 1‑15:

[A publication]
may be defamatory in its plain and ordinary meaning or by virtue of extrinsic
facts or circumstances, known to the listener or reader, which give it a
defamatory meaning by way of innuendo different from that in which it
ordinarily would be understood.

Qualified Privilege

[
90
]

The Supreme Court reviewed the defence of qualified privilege in
Hill
v. Church of Scientology of Toronto
,
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1130, 126 D.L.R.
(4th) 129 [
Hill
], and the principles set out in that case can be
summarized as follows:

(a)        Qualified
privilege attaches to an occasion where the person who makes the communication
has an interest, or duty, legal, social, or moral, to make it to the person to
whom it is made, and the person to whom it is so made has a corresponding
interest or duty to receive it. (at para. 143)

(b)        The
privilege is not absolute and can be defeated if the dominant motive for
publishing the statement is actual or express malice. The legal effect of the
defence of qualified privilege rebuts the inference that normally arises from
the publication of defamatory words, which is that they were spoken with
malice. The onus of proving express or actual malice rests with the plaintiff.
(at para. 144)

(c)        Malice
is commonly understood, in the popular sense, as spite or ill-will. However, it
also includes any indirect motive or ulterior purpose that conflicts with the
sense of duty or the mutual interest created by the occasion. Malice may also
be established by showing that the defendant spoke dishonestly, or in knowing
or reckless disregard for the truth. (at para. 145)

(d)        Qualified
privilege may also be defeated when the limits of the duty or interest have
been exceeded, and the information communicated is not reasonably appropriate
in the context of the circumstances existing on the occasion when given. (at paras.
146-147)

[
91
]

The trial judge correctly stated the applicable principles of law, and
the appellant does not allege any error of law in this regard.

[
92

[
93

[
94

was not defamatory because it was true. We disagree. The trial judge declined
to make any finding on the correctness of Dr. Cadsky’s opinion. In our view,
the trial judge concluded that the statement was defamatory, and went on to
consider the defence of qualified privilege.

[
95
]

The trial judge concluded that Dr. Cadsky, as admitted by him, referred
to Dr. Chohan as the “paranoid Sikh.” The trial judge did not accept the
evidence of Drs. Woods and Rai that Dr. Cadsky stated that he intended or
planned to provoke an argument with Dr. Chohan and thus force him to leave
FACS. He accepted Dr. Cadsky’s evidence that he did not make that statement but
that he likely stated something to the effect that it would not take much for
Dr. Chohan to leave FACS, given his reputation for being short tempered with
his supervisors, and for quitting positions as a result.

[
96
]

The appellant challenges this finding and says that it is palpably
wrong. We disagree. The trial judge is in the best position to judge
credibility. Drs. Rai and Woods testified as to their memory of what was said
by Dr. Cadsky. They made no notes of the conversation, and were relying
entirely on their memory when they first discussed it with Dr. Chohan over a
month later. Dr. Rai first made a written record of the conversation in a
letter addressed to Dr. Gardener dated March 27, 2004, more than a year later.
At trial, neither Dr. Woods nor Dr. Rai could recall the circumstances in which
the statement was made. The appellant also relies on the evidence of Dr.
Santana, who testified that Dr. Tweddle told him that once FACS had a full
complement of staff, Dr. Cadsky would make sure that Dr. Chohan left. Dr.
Tweddle denied making such a statement. Dr. Cadsky denied ever stating that he
would make Dr. Chohan leave. Dr. Chohan testified that Dr. Cadsky always
treated him with respect. There was no evidence that, in the period of
approximately one year after the statement was made and the discovery by Dr.
Cadsky that Dr. Chohan had been told of his “paranoid Sikh” comment, that Dr.
Cadsky attempted to provoke any argument with Dr. Chohan. In fact, they
appeared to avoid each other unless necessary. Having reviewed the evidence, we
conclude that there is evidence to support the trial judge’s finding and that
it is not reversible on appeal.

[
97
]

The appellant also challenges the trial judge’s finding that Dr.
Cadsky’s statement was not racially motivated. He submits that on its face, the
statement has racial connotations. The appellant also points to Dr. Cadsky’s
use of the word “epithet” in his explanation at trial where he said: “Sikh was
simply because that was the most glaringly obvious epithet to describe his
appearance.” While the word “epithet” can signify a term of abuse, the first
dictionary meaning is “an adjective or descriptive word expressing a quality or
attribute.” In any event, the balance of Dr. Cadsky’s evidence referring to his
use of “Sikh” indicated that he intended to identify Dr. Chohan by appearance.
The finding was open on the evidence, especially when considered in the context
of the whole of the evidence, which established that Dr. Cadsky exhibited no
tendency to discriminate on racial or religious grounds. Other than the
statement about the other psychiatrist, there was no evidence of any incident
suggestive of racism. On the contrary, as found by the trial judge, the
evidence suggested that Dr. Cadsky was accommodating and generous to medical
staff from a variety of racial and religious backgrounds. The trial judge found
that Dr. Cadsky’s rhetoric was out of keeping with his actions. We cannot say
that he was palpably wrong to do so.

Qualified Privilege

[
98
]

The appellant says that the trial judge erred in concluding that the
occasion was one of qualified privilege as Dr. Cadsky had no legal, social, or
moral duty or interest to make the statement to Drs. Woods and Rai. At the
time, Dr. Cadsky had been removed from his position as clinical coordinator,
was on stress leave, and had no official role in the running of FACS. The
appellant submits that Dr. Woods and Dr. Rai were there on a social visit, and
may have sought his views about the possible candidates to replace Dr. Brooks,
but not his assessment of Dr. Chohan’s mental condition.

[
99
]

The trial judge found that the occasion was one that attracted qualified
privilege. The occasion involved a discussion among three psychiatrists who
were practising their profession at FACS. Dr. Cadsky was on stress leave from
FACS when the two junior doctors came to visit him Although Dr. Cadsky was not
the clinical coordinator, he was a senior psychiatrist and had been performing
many of the duties of clinical coordinator. The clinical director position was
about to become vacant. Each of the psychiatrists had a legitimate interest to
frankly discuss possible candidates and the strengths and weaknesses of the
candidates. Nothing requires that the persons with interest be in a position to
make or influence the decision. The trial judge found that although Dr.
Cadsky’s statement was inappropriate and inflammatory, the context in which it
was made indicated that qualified privilege applied. In fact, Dr. Cadsky’s
position had not changed substantially, as is clear from the evidence of Dr.
Rai, whose primary interest in visiting Dr. Cadsky was to ascertain his views
on a position that had been offered to Dr. Rai. Conversations between
colleagues expressing opinions on other employees’ qualifications are precisely
the sort of communications that the defence of qualified privilege was designed
to protect. The trial judge correctly stated the test, made findings of fact
that were open to him on the evidence, and properly applied the test. He
correctly concluded that the occasion was one of privilege.

Malice

[
100
]

The
trial judge made a number of fact findings that govern his conclusion in that
malice had not been established. First, he found that Dr. Cadsky honestly
believed that, on a certain level, Dr. Chohan had exhibited conduct that could
support the conclusion of paranoia. This finding negated any suggestion that
Dr. Cadsky spoke dishonestly, or that he knowingly or recklessly disregarded
the truth. Dr. Cadsky testified that Dr. Chohan exhibited four of the seven
criteria associated with a paranoid personality: (1) he was quick to perceive
attacks on his character, and quick to overreact and fight back; (2) he read
demeaning or threatening messages into otherwise ordinary comments; (3) he bore
grudges, and could not let go of perceived insults or slights; and (4) he
believed others were out to harm him. Dr. Cadsky believed that these traits had
no effect on Dr. Chohan’s ability to practise psychiatry, and consistently
advised and testified that Dr. Chohan’s ability as a psychiatrist was of the
highest quality. This is confirmed by Dr. Friend’s evidence, who had knowledge
of Dr. Chohan’s performance reviews over his career at FACS, in respect of
which Dr. Cadsky had some input and testified that those reviews were always
good. However, Dr. Cadsky found Dr. Chohan to be a difficult colleague.

[
101
]

The
trial judge found that the remarks, although phrased in racial terms, and were
reasonably understood by Drs. Woods and Rai to be racist, were not racially
motivated and were not intended to be defamatory. He relied on evidence that
established Dr. Cadsky to be blunt and inappropriate in his speech, though he
was generous and accommodating to colleagues in FACS, many of whom represented
a variety of backgrounds and races. This finding was supported by the evidence
of Dr. Rai, a person of Sikh background, who conceded that Dr. Cadsky had been
very supportive and generous to him when he and his family moved to Edmonton at
the commencement of his employment. It was also supported by Dr. Chohan’s
evidence. He testified that Dr. Cadsky had always been respectful in his
dealings with him. Dr. Tweddle described Dr. Cadsky as “not racist,” and
explained: “He’s often sort of big‑footed, rude and obnoxious, but he is
equally like that with everyone.”

[
102
]

As
indicated by the trial judge, Dr. Cadsky’s unfortunate choice of language did
not fairly correspond to his generosity in dealings with his colleagues. The
trial judge accepted Dr. Cadsky’s evidence that he was referring only to
description when he used the word “Sikh” and that the “paranoid” description
was Dr. Cadsky’s honest opinion, based largely on information regarding Dr.
Chohan’s dealings with others. The trial judge concluded: “I find that the
statement he made to Drs. Rai and Woods was not malicious, but was conveyed in
the context of a frank discussion of the leadership qualities (or lack thereof)
of various individuals in anticipation of a leadership vacuum.”

[
103
]

In
discussing the malice issue, the trial judge did not refer to two letters
written by Dr. Cadsky, which the appellant submits demonstrate malice. In April
2003, Dr. Cadsky composed a draft letter to the College of Physicians and
Surgeons, complaining about Dr. Chohan’s opposition to his reinstatement and
what he claimed were other attacks on him by Dr. Chohan. He never sent this
letter but retained it as his notes of what occurred. He gave copies to Dr.
Ohlhauser and Dr. Mador when interviewed by them in 2004. Although the
appellant describes this letter as disparaging, it says nothing about the
paranoia statement. Rather it contains a list of events that Dr. Cadsky
describes as defamatory of him, including efforts to effect the termination of
Dr. Cadsky’s position as Clinical Coordinator. We see nothing in that letter
that reflects on Dr. Cadsky’s motives in making the paranoid Sikh comment. In a
memorandum dated July 30, 2004, Dr. Cadsky reported to Dr. Dempsey on an
encounter with Dr. Chohan at FACS and stated that he was concerned that the
circumstances “may imply a deterioration of his mental status.” This letter was
written more than 15 months after the defamatory comments, a period filled with
calls for Dr. Cadsky’s removal, complaints to Dr. Gardener, Sheila Weatherill,
and the Board of Capital Health, a complaint to the Human Rights Commission,
and two internal investigations. Having regard to what occurred in the interim,
it is difficult to see what relevance comments made after those events could
have in deciding on motives in making a statement, some 15 months earlier.

[
104
]

The
appellant submits that the trial judge failed to comprehend the meaning and
context of the words “paranoid Sikh,” and says that the words were intended to
be derogatory, and convey a particular and negative connotation: “That they
conveyed a harmful stereotype - one of a foreigner who is irrational, angry,
aggressive, hostile and extremist.” We do not agree. The trial judge correctly
concluded that Dr. Cadsky intended to convey to his listeners his honestly held
opinion that because of what he saw as paranoia, Dr. Chohan would not be a
suitable candidate for the administrative position under discussion. Dr. Cadsky
voiced opinions in respect of each of the psychiatrists practising at FACS, and
concluded that none would be suitable for the position of Clinical Director.
The evidence did not support the conclusion that Dr. Cadsky spoke with spite, ill
will, with an ulterior purpose, or dishonestly. Whether malice has been
established is a question of mixed law and fact that is heavily dependent on
fact findings, and reviewable on a standard of palpable and overriding error.
In interpreting the words used, the trial judge relied on the whole of the
evidence before him, which did not support the conclusion suggested by the
appellant.

Limits to Qualified
Privilege

[
105
]

The
fourth criterion established by the Supreme Court in
Hill
at
paras.
146‑147
asks whether the limits of the duty have been exceeded:

Qualified privilege may also be
defeated when the limits of the duty or interest have been exceeded. ... As
Loreburn E. stated at pp. 320-21 in
Adam v. Ward
,
supra
:

... the fact
that an occasion is privileged does not necessarily protect all that is said or
written on that occasion. Anything that is not relevant and pertinent to the
discharge of the duty or the exercise of the right or the safeguarding of the
interest which creates the privilege will not be protected.

In other
words, the information communicated must be reasonably appropriate in the
context of the circumstances existing on the occasion when that information was
given.

[
106
]

In

Hill
, Manning, a senior lawyer, wearing his robes and accompanied
by representatives of his client, the Church of Scientology, held a press
conference on the steps of Osgoode Hall. The press conference had been arranged
by his client and was attended by representatives from several media organizations,
giving it the widest possible dissemination. He read from and commented on
allegations in a Notice of Motion, by which the Church of Scientology intended
to commence criminal contempt proceedings against Hill, then Crown Counsel. The
Notice of Motion alleged that Hill had misled a judge and breached court orders
sealing certain documents, serious allegations of misconduct against another
lawyer. The allegations were false. The Supreme Court confirmed that privilege
applies to the reporting of court proceedings and court documents; however
found that Manning’s conduct far exceeded the legitimate purposes of the
occasion. The circumstances of the case required great restraint in the
communication of the information concerning the proceedings. Manning should
have taken steps to confirm the allegations in the Notice of Motion,
particularly since he knew that his client was investigating the allegations
regarding the access to the sealed documents and that the investigation to date
had not confirmed that any sealed documents had been opened. In the
circumstances, he was bound to await the result of the investigation before
making any comment. The permissible scope of his comments was limited as a
result of his failure to take the reasonable steps, and his failure defeated
the qualified privilege that attached to the occasion. The information
contained unproven and unverified allegations of serious professional
misconduct, and was made in language that portrayed Hill in the worst possible
light and was given the widest possible dissemination. Cory J. did not find it
necessary to characterize Manning’s conduct as actual malice but concluded that
it was high-handed and careless. He concluded that conduct was neither
necessary nor appropriate in the circumstances and defeated the qualified
privilege that attached to the occasion. The decision in
Hill

requires courts to carefully examine all the circumstances and decide whether
the communication was necessary and appropriate in the circumstances, or
whether it exceeded the legitimate purposes of the occasion.

[
107
]

The
appellant submits that qualified privilege was defeated because Dr. Cadsky
exceeded the limits of the duty or interest being protected as the use of the
word “Sikh” was not appropriate in this context and was not relevant to Dr.
Chohan’s qualities or suitability as a psychiatrist or potential supervisor.
The issue of whether qualified privilege was defeated on this ground was not
specifically addressed by the trial judge, and after reviewing the written
arguments presented to the trial judge, we do not believe that it was argued
before him.

[
108
]

Here,
the occasion to which privilege attached was a private discussion between three
psychiatrists concerning the suitability of a number of their colleagues to fill
the position of Clinical Director of Forensic Services, their supervisor. The
audience was limited and Dr. Cadsky had no reason to believe that the
information would be communicated to anyone else. The trial judge found as a
fact that Dr. Cadsky used the word “Sikh” as identification and that the
statement communicated Dr. Cadsky’s honest opinion about the suitability of
Dr.Chohan, one of the possible candidates, to fill that position. As found by
the trial judge, the language was offensive and intemperate. Undoubtedly, Dr.
Cadsky could have found many better ways to express his opinion. However, the
choice of inappropriate language does not defeat qualified privilege, if the
occasion is privileged and the statement is relevant to the protected interest.

[
109
]

The
appeal against the dismissal of the action against Dr. Cadsky is dismissed.

Other Defendants

[
110
]

We
dismiss the appeals against Dr. Ohlhauser, Dr. Baker, Dr. Gardener and Capital
Health, as we are not persuaded that the trial judge made any reversible error
in dismissing those actions. We will address the arguments separately, but
commence with the following summary. Dr. Ohlhauser, Dr. Baker, and Dr. Gardener
each testified that as a result of expressions of concern from others and/or their
personal observations, each had an honest concern about the health of a
colleague, and believed that, as a medical professional, he had a duty to
either investigate this concern, or inform someone who was in a position to
investigate. Each contacted the person he believed appropriate to provide
assistance or investigate to ensure that there was no cause for concern. There
is no evidence that any one of them contacted individuals who had no interest
in knowing and no responsibility to receive the communication because of the
position he held in Capital Health. Dr. Block, Dr. Hibbert and Dr. Gardener,
the three persons to whom communications were made, each had a responsibility
for ensuring that colleagues within their service did not have health issues that
might affect patient care or their own well being. These three defendants were
not engaged in idle gossip or general discussion in making these
communications. In our view, the defence of qualified privilege was designed
for exactly such a situation.

Dr. Baker

[
111
]

In
assessing Dr. Baker’s liability, the trial judge accepted his evidence that he
would not have used the term “paranoid” to refer to Dr. Chohan when speaking to
Dr. Block. Accordingly, the trial judge found that his communication to Dr.
Block was not defamatory. In the alternative, the trial judge concluded that
even if the statement were defamatory, it was made on an occasion of qualified
privilege and it was not motivated by malice.

[
112
]

The
appellant says that the trial judge erred in finding that Dr. Baker did not say
that Dr. Chohan was, or may be, paranoid. He submits that the evidence of Dr.
Block should have been accepted. In his evidence, Dr. Block recalls that Drs.
Baker and Ohlhauser both used the word “paranoid.” Dr. Baker explained why he would
not have used a psychiatric term in discussions with psychiatrists, and the
trial judge was entitled to accept his evidence. This court cannot overrule the
trial judge’s conclusion on credibility and reliability of the conflicting
evidence before him.

[
113
]

Dr.
Baker contacted Dr. Chohan on June 13, 2003, and made an appointment with him
for June 25 to discuss his project involving an academic forensic division as
part of the University of Alberta Psychiatry program. At their meeting, Dr.
Baker found that Dr. Chohan focussed on his complaints to Capital Health and
that he was excessively upset and angry about the lack any of action by Dr.
Gardener to resolve his complaints. Dr. Baker testified that little time was
spent discussing the project, as Dr. Chohan kept returning to his problems with
Capital Health. As a result of this meeting, Dr. Baker became concerned about
Dr. Chohan’s well-being. He talked to Dr. Ohlhauser, who he knew also met with
Dr. Chohan, and confirmed that Dr. Ohlhauser had similar concerns. Dr. Baker
testified that he believed that he had a responsibility to let Dr. Block know
about his concerns. Accordingly, he phoned Dr. Block and informed him of his
concerns. After receiving Dr. Block’s assurance, Dr. Baker contacted Dr.
Gardener as well.

[
114
]

We
do not consider it relevant whether Dr. Baker used the term “paranoid” in his
communications with Dr. Block and Dr. Gardener, or merely expressed concern
about Dr. Chohan’s level of distress over the delay in resolving his
complaints. Nonetheless, we note that the finding made by the trial judge was
supported by evidence, and he was entitled to accept Dr. Baker’s evidence. His
factual finding is not open to review by this court.

[
115
]

The
appellant submits that qualified privilege did not apply because Dr. Baker had
no legal, social, or moral duty or interest to make the statement to Dr. Block
on that occasion; that he had no role to play in Capital Health and no mandate
to deal with the issue. We do not agree. Dr. Baker was, at the relevant time,
the Chair of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Alberta. Dr.
Chohan held a position there as a clinical lecturer. That relationship clearly
gave Dr. Baker a duty, responsibility and interest in communicating his
concerns to the person who would be in the best position to address those
concerns, namely Dr. Block, who was the head of the Department of Psychiatry
where Dr. Chohan practised. Dr. Block agreed that it was part of his responsibility
to receive, investigate and address any such concerns. Dr. Baker also
communicated with Dr. Gardener. While that communication may not have been
strictly necessary, Dr. Baker believed that Dr. Gardener should be aware of the
concerns.

[
116
]

We
are not persuaded that Dr. Baker exceeded the limits of the duty or interest
that arose as a result of his concerns. Dr. Baker communicated his concerns to
the two individuals who were responsible for psychiatric staff at the Royal
Alexandra Hospital. The trial judge made no error in concluding that qualified
privilege protected Dr. Baker’s communications with Drs. Block and Gardener.

Dr. Ohlhauser

[
117
]

The
appellant submits that the trial judge erred in finding that Dr. Ohlhauser was
protected by qualified privilege in respect of his communication with Dr.
Hibbard and Dr. Gardener. The appellant says that as Dr. Ohlhauser was not
involved with Capital Health at the time of the communications, and was not a
practising physician, he had no duty or interest. The appellant describes Dr.
Ohlhauser as meddling, and submits that Dr. Ohlhauser exceeded the limits of
any duty he may have had.

[
118
]

Dr.
Ohlhauser had received information from Dr. King, a friend of Dr. Chohan and a
reputable psychiatrist, that Dr. Chohan was overreacting to the failure of
Capital Health and Dr. Gardener to resolve his complaints, and that he may be
paranoid. Dr. Ohlhauser suggested that Dr. King contact the College and get
their assistance. Dr. King did not wish to follow that route. Dr. Ohlhauser
confirmed that information with Dr. Metelitsa. Following his discussion with
Dr. Metelitsa, Dr. Ohlhauser advised Dr. King that he would try to assist. He
asked Dr. King to recommend a psychiatrist who could assist in providing an
assessment and support, and asked Dr. King to have Dr. Chohan telephone him if
he wanted to talk to Dr. Ohlhauser. Dr. King recommended that he contact Dr.
Hibbard who worked at the Royal Alexandra Hospital with Dr. Chohan. Dr.
Ohlhauser’s messages to Dr. Hibbard were intended to obtain his support and
assessment, if needed.

[
119
]

The
details of the conversation are set out in the trial judge’s reasons. Suffice
it to say that Dr. Chohan was seeking to have Dr. Ohlhauser assist him in
resolving his complaints. Dr. Ohlhauser focussed on assessing Dr. Chohan’s
state of health and on encouraging him to find other solutions for his concerns
so as not to damage his career. At the conclusion of their meeting, Dr.
Ohlhauser confirmed that Dr. Chohan was upset and agitated, and that some assessment
was required.

[
120
]

The
appellant submits that the trial judge erred in accepting Dr. Ohlhauser’s
evidence and, at one point, accuses Dr. Ohlhauser of fabricating statements
attributed to Drs. King and Metelitsa. We do not agree. Dr. Ohlhauser’s
evidence about his discussions with Dr. King was (with one exception) confirmed
by Dr. King’s testimony. The only conflict in their evidence is whether or not
Dr. Ohlhauser confirmed with Dr. King that he was talking about clinical
paranoia or using the term in its general sense. That aside, Dr. Ohlhauser
testified that he met Dr. Metelitsa following his discussion with Dr. King, and
confirmed that Dr. Metelitsa shared Dr. King’s concerns about paranoia, and
that he would not have become involved without this confirmation. Dr. Metelitsa
denied that this meeting occurred and that he had ever any concerns about Dr.
Chohan’s state of health. Dr. King confirmed Dr. Metelitsa’s involvement, and
testified that he and Dr. Metelitsa were both concerned about Dr. Chohan’s
overreaction to the lack of a satisfactory response from Capital Health to his
complaints, and that he would harm his career. Dr. King says that Dr. Metelitsa
agreed that Dr. King should approach Dr. Ohlhauser. There was evidence to
support the fact findings made by the trial judge, and we see nothing
unreasonable in his conclusion in light of this evidence.

[
121
]

As
submitted by the appellant, the trial judge erred in stating (at para. 280)
that Dr. Ohlhauser did not learn of Dr. Cadsky’s “paranoid Sikh” comment until
September 2003. The trial judge obviously misspoke when he made that statement,
as he had earlier referred to Dr. Ohlhauser’s evidence that Dr. Chohan had told
him about Dr. Cadsky’s “paranoid Sikh” comment on June 27. In cross-examination,
Dr. Ohlhauser stated that he was not sure when he first learned about the
comment.

[
122
]

While
the appellant suggests that this error undermines the factual underpinnings of
the trial judge’s conclusions, we do not agree. The trial judge accepted Dr.
Ohlhauser’s evidence regarding the concerns expressed by Drs. King and
Metelitsa. At the time of the first call to Dr. Hibbard, Dr. Ohlhauser knew
that Drs. King and Metelitsa were concerned that Dr. Chohan was overreacting
and paranoid. While he used the term “sick doc” in his first message to Dr.
Hibbard, Dr. Ohlhauser did not identify the individual by name. By the
conclusion of his meeting with Dr. Chohan, Dr. Ohlhauser confirmed from his own
observations the information he received from Drs. King and Metelitsa. He then
left a message on a private voice mail service, identifying Dr. Chohan and
indicating that “he may be paranoid” and asking for help. Dr. Ohlhauser’s
knowledge of the details of Dr. Chohan’s complaint against Dr. Cadsky does not
detract from his concerns about Dr. Chohan’s state of health and the need to
have an assessment.

[
123
]

We
agree with the trial judge that Dr. Ohlhauser, as a senior physician, had a
duty to communicate the information once he learned of, and confirmed, the
concerns. The appellant submits that if Dr. Ohlhauser had a duty, it was to
investigate cautiously. We agree with this submission, although we do not agree
that Dr. Ohlhauser did not investigate cautiously. He telephoned the
psychiatrist who had been identified by Dr. King as being able to help. He did
not state that Dr. Chohan was paranoid, but rather indicated that he “may” be
and asked whether Dr. Hibbard was willing to help. When Dr. Hibbard did not
return his call, Dr. Ohlhauser called Dr. Gardener and explained his concerns
to him. We agree with the appellant’s submission that both Drs. Hibbard and
Gardener took the statements seriously.

[
124
]

The
appellant complains that Dr. Ohlhauser did not tell Dr. Gardener about Dr.
Cadsky’s comment and submits that this is evidence of “an approach to Dr.
Chohan that is both incompetent and biased.” The appellant submits that Dr.
Ohlhauser had an obligation to alert Dr. Gardener about Dr. Chohan’s specific
concerns about Dr. Cadsky. We do not agree. There is no evidence to suggest
that Dr. Ohlhauser knew, or should have known, that Dr. Chohan had not told Dr.
Gardener about Dr. Cadsky’s comment. That question was not put to him in cross
examination, and there is nothing to suggest that he should have known, nor
that communication of Dr. Chohan’s complaints formed any part of his
responsibility. His only obligation was to advise Dr. Gardener about his
concerns, and to leave the rest to Dr. Gardener. That he did.

[
125
]

We
agree with the trial judge’s conclusion that malice has not been established.
The appellant submits that malice is established by two facts: (1) Dr.
Ohlhauser did not decline the role offered to him to act as consultant “when he
ought to have appreciated that he could not be viewed as a fair-minded arbiter
in the circumstances,” and (2) Dr. Ohlhauser failed “to tell Dr. Gardener that
he knew the source of the false paranoid notion” was Dr. Cadsky. We find no
evidence to support either position.

[
126
]

We
find there is no evidence to support the proposition that Dr. Ohlhauser knew or
should have known that he could not be considered a fair-minded arbiter.
Further, the evidence does not support the suggestion that consultation
agreement required that he have no prior knowledge of the situation at FACS.
He was invited to participate because of his interest in mental health and
reputation, and to assist the administration and the psychiatrists in resolving
the issues and in planning for the future. The suggestion that he had a
predetermined view that compromised his neutrality or ability to accomplish the
task assigned to him is not supported by the evidence. Dr. Ohlhauser had some
concerns arising from the statements made by Drs. King and Metelitsa, as well
as from his own observations. He believed that he had a duty to draw those
concerns to the attention of someone in authority so that Dr. Chohan’s
condition could be assessed and he did so. He was subsequently advised by Dr.
Gardener that Dr. Block had no concerns about Dr. Chohan’s state of health.
Nothing in the evidence suggests that Dr. Ohlhauser persisted in his concerns
about Dr. Chohan’s state of health following Dr. Gardener’s statement to him.
In any event, Dr. Ohlhauser’s task at FACS did not involve a determination of
any question involving Dr. Chohan’s state of health.

[
127
]

The
evidence also does not support the appellant’s suggestion that the source of
the false paranoid notion was Dr. Cadsky. Other than the disclosure to Dr.
Chohan, there is no evidence that Dr. Cadsky’s “paranoid Sihk” comment was
repeated by either of the two recipients until March 2004, well after Dr.
Ohlhauser’s June meeting with Dr. Chohan. Nor was it repeated by Dr. Cadsky.
There was no further communication of the comment except by Dr. Chohan, who
discussed it with his colleagues in the group. Dr. Chohan does not suggest that
the comment became general knowledge. The evidence established that Dr. King
expressed concern about paranoia when he spoke to Dr. Ohlhauser. Dr. Chohan may
have told him about Dr. Cadsky’s comment. However, there is no suggestion in
Dr. King’s evidence that he was adopting or repeating Dr. Cadsky’s view. Dr.
King had formed his own opinion, based on his own observations of Dr. Chohan’s
actions and emotional state.

[
128
]

The
trial judge correctly identified the occasion as one of qualified privilege.
His conclusion that there was no malice on the part of Dr. Ohlhauser is
supported by the evidence. We therefore dismiss the appeal of the action
against Dr. Ohlhauser.

Dr. Gardener

[
129
]

The
only communication by Dr. Gardener pled as defamatory was his phone call to Dr.
Block, in which Dr. Gardener stated that he had received information expressing
concerns that Dr. Chohan may be paranoid. As the Chief Medical Officer at
Capital Health, Dr. Gardener had responsibility for ensuring the competence and
well-being of the physicians practising in the Capital Health system. Having
received phone calls from Drs. Baker and Ohlhauser expressing the concerns, Dr.
Gardener believed that he had an obligation to make an inquiry. Dr. Gardener
would have been neglecting his duties to Capital Health and his ethical
obligations as a physician if he simply ignored the information, as the
appellant suggests he should have done. He contacted Dr. Block, the Chief of
the Psychiatric Service where Dr. Chohan practised, who was the appropriate
person to receive the information. The occasion was clearly one to which
qualified privilege attached.

[
130
]

To
succeed, the appellant must prove actual malice. The trial judge correctly
concluded that there was no evidence of actual malice. The appellant suggests
that actual malice has been proven based on the following:

(1) Dr. Gardener contracted with
Dr. Ohlhauser knowing that he had a predetermined adverse opinion of Dr.
Chohan.

(2) Dr. Gardener established an
irregular review committee when “he realized that Dr. Ohlhauser’s involvement
had failed and that he could no longer claim not to know that many of the toxic
workplace issues could be traced back to Dr. Cadsky’s slander and threats.”

(3) Dr. Gardener appointed persons
to the committee who could be seen as having a conflict of interest (as two of
them had participated in the decision to reinstate Dr. Cadsky), all in the face
of expressed concerns.

(4) Dr. Gardener failed to follow
Capital Health’s Workplace Respect Policy in dealing with the complaint.

(5) That following the report and
recommendation of the review committee, Dr. Gardener placed on Dr. Chohan’s
file at the Alberta Hospital Edmonton the letter sent to him on December 10,
2004, which the appellant says was written long after Dr. Gardener knew that
the contents were not true.

[
131
]

Dealing
first with Dr. Ohlhauser’s appointment, we find nothing to suggest that Dr.
Ohlhauser had formed any predetermined adverse view of Dr. Chohan or the state
of his mental health, or that Dr. Gardener knew or should have known about it.
Dr. Ohlhauser, after hearing from Drs. King and Metelitsa, and following his
meeting with Dr. Chohan, became concerned. As result of his concerns, Dr.
Ohlhauser took steps to first seek the assistance of a psychiatrist as a
support person to determine whether a mental health issue existed. Having
received no response from Dr. Hibbard, he telephoned Dr. Gardener to advise of
his concerns. In any event, Dr. Ohlhauser was appointed to assist in resolving
the disputes between the two factions of psychiatrists in FACS, and to assist
in planning a future program; he was not appointed to assume a judicial or quasi-judicial
role involving the determination of Dr. Chohan’s state of health, as reflected
by Dr. Ohlhauser’s role in subsequent meetings and discussions with the
psychiatrists.

[
132
]

The
next three allegations relate to the committee appointed by Dr. Gardener. The
appellant submits that Eleanor Grant and Dr. Brahim were “disqualified” because
they had been involved in the reinstatement of Dr. Cadsky. In our view,
involvement in the reinstatement of Dr. Cadsky, pursuant to the settlement of
his legal action, did not disqualify these two individuals.

[
133
]

Dr.
Gardener also testified that the workplace complaint procedure was not
appropriate as the concerns were not limited to a single complaint or incident
as was appropriate for that procedure. Rather, the concerns involved a number
of issues raised by different psychiatrists, as indicated in Dr. Chohan’s
letter of April 2, 2004. Dr. Gardener sought a procedure that would identify
and address all incidents underlying the generalized complaints, and decided
that a committee of senior Capital Health Executives not directly involved in
FACS, together with the President of the Medical Staff would be most
appropriate. Dr. Gardener advised the FACS psychiatrists that changes to the
committee could be made, provided that concerns about the individuals who had
been appointed were clearly set out in writing. No written concerns were
expressed by any of the psychiatrists, including Dr. Chohan.

[
134
]

At
trial, Dr. Chohan testified that prior to the commencement of the Committee’s
interviews, Eleanor Grant stated to Dr. Block that Dr. Chohan was paranoid
because he had written to all Capital Health Board Members. Dr. Block testified
at trial but was not asked about this conversation. In any event, neither Dr.
Block nor Dr. Chohan disclosed any concerns about Eleanor Grant’s qualification
to serve on the Committee to Dr. Gardener, in writing or otherwise. Dr. Chohan
simply refused to participate. On April 19, Drs. Metelitsa, Rai, Santana and
Woods wrote to Sheila Weatherill regarding the process. They raised no
objection regarding any individual committee member, but set out their
complaints regarding Dr. Gardener’s refusal to exclude the “intimidators” and
others who had nothing to do with the issues from the meeting, and his refusal
to respect their requests for a confidential meeting. They concluded: “we
cannot see how we can have any confidence in a committee authorised by Dr.
Gardener.”

[
135
]

Ms.
Weatherill responded by expressing confidence in Dr. Gardener, and indicated
that she had personally approved all three members of the committee, each of
whom was a senior member of Capital Health’s executive team. She reiterated
that if they knew of any reason why any member of the committee should not
serve, they should advise Dr. Gardener and “their membership will be reviewed.”
She also suggested that additional members could be appointed if it would be
helpful. No changes were requested.

[
136
]

The
evidence does not support the suggestion that Dr. Gardener, knowingly appointed
an irregular committee.

[
137
]

The
committee conducted private interviews with the FACS psychiatrists (other than
Dr. Chohan) and other staff. All who participated were assured that their
communications would be treated as confidential, as requested by a number of
the psychiatrists. The committee submitted its report to Dr. Gardener, and made
numerous recommendations, including that Dr. Cadsky be reprimanded, and that
Dr. Gardener meet with Dr. Chohan to ensure that he continued to have support.

[
138
]

After
unsuccessfully attempting to discuss the committee’s recommendation with Dr.
Chohan at a meeting, Dr. Gardener wrote to Dr. Chohan on December 10, 2004,
thanking him for attending and adding:

As I indicated at our meeting, I
continue to have concerns that the circumstances of the past couple of years
have affected your health. I encourage you to make sure you are adequately
supported by either a family physician or a colleague in the mental health
field.

[
139
]

The
appellant submits that this letter is evidence of malice, as Dr. Gardener knew
that the appellant had no mental health problems but wrote a letter that can
only be understood as a signal to any reader that he had such problems. This
letter was placed on Dr. Chohan’s file at the Alberta Hospital Edmonton.

[
140
]

It
is not clear whether the appellant argued at trial that the subsequent letter
demonstrated malice at the time of the publication of the defamatory material.
The trial judge makes no mention of the letter when discussing this issue, and
makes no finding as to its significance. The trial judge did conclude that
there was no evidence of malice on the part of Dr. Gardener.

[
141
]

Although
malice may be proven by subsequent events, the issue requires a finding of the
state of mind of the speaker at the time the defamatory statement was made.
Nothing in the December 10 letter could reasonably lead to the conclusion that
some months earlier, when Dr. Gardener phoned Dr. Block, he was motivated by
spite, ill will, or some indirect motive or ulterior purpose that conflicts with
the sense of duty the occasion created. Nor can it establish that, at that
time, Dr. Gardener spoke dishonestly or in reckless disregard of the truth. The
evidence of Dr. Gardener’s intention and motivation when he called Dr. Block
was clear, as we have earlier indicated. We agree with the trial judge that
there is no evidence of malice on the part of Dr. Gardener.

[
142
]

The
appeal against the dismissal of the action against Dr. Gardener and Capital
Health is dismissed.

General

[
143
]

The
appellant suggests that the trial judge became unduly distracted by the
workplace issues taking place at the time the impugned statements were made. In
our view, it is impossible to separate the defamatory statements alleged from
the workplace issues. They not only provide the setting for the subsequent
activity of all parties, but were the central core of the complaints being
forwarded to Dr. Gardener and Capital Health by Dr. Chohan and the other
psychiatrists, as is evident from all correspondence leading up to the April 4,
2004 letter from Dr. Chohan to Dr. Gardener. The trial judge was careful in his
reasons to segregate issues relating to defamation from the general concerns
about leadership, harassment, and intimidation.

[
144
]

Whatever
difficulty existed between the two factions of psychiatrists at FACS it was not
caused by Dr. Cadsky’s statement. The problem existed before the statement, and
resulted from a dissatisfaction by some with leadership issues and accusations
of intimidation and harassment, none of which were defined by specific
instances that could provide a foundation for the complaints. Dr. Chohan’s
professional reputation remained intact throughout, and he continued to be held
in highest esteem by his colleagues. Some of his professional colleagues became
concerned about his own reaction to his inability to obtain redress for his
complaints. Some of his colleagues knew of Dr. Cadsky’s statement. Others did
not. The evidence of Dr. King, Dr. Ohlhauser, Dr. Baker and Dr. Gardener
demonstrates their genuine concern (some based on their own observations,
others on credible information) that a respected colleague may be overreacting
to the situation, and wishing to ensure his well-being. Those who knew of the
“paranoid Sikh” comment simply disregarded it.

[
145
]

Because
we are dismissing the appeal, we need not deal with any issues relating to
damages. The trial judge assessed “nominal damages” at $5000. Having regard to
the finding that there was little discernable harm to Dr. Chohan’s reputation,
but that the events caused him great emotional distress, the provisional
assessment of damages of $5000 is not out of line, although we would not
describe them as “nominal.”

Costs

[
146
]

The
appellant also seeks to have costs awarded to the other parties set aside. He
does so on grounds that the trial judge:

(1) failed to request submissions
and failed to have regard to the criteria in Rule 601(1),

(2) blamed the appellant for an
unnecessarily long trial, and

(3) failed to consider pre‑litigation
misconduct.

[
147
]

The
appellant cites Dr. Gardener’s December 10, 2004 letter as evidence of such
misconduct, on the basis that Dr. Gardener knew that there was no basis for any
concerns about mental illness when he wrote the letter. The December letter
does not indicate that Dr. Chohan had previously suffered from mental illness,
nor that he was then suffering from a mental illness. Dr. Gardener’s concerns
were that the circumstances of the last two years may have affected Dr.
Chohan’s health, and he encouraged Dr. Chohan to ensure that he was supported
by either a family physician or a colleague in mental health. That letter
remains on Dr. Chohan’s file at the Alberta Hospital. In his evidence, Dr.
Gardener did not refer to paranoia or mental health issues. He stated that he
was concerned about the effects that the last couple of years had had on Dr.
Chohan’s health. Witnesses, including Dr. Chohan, described the lengthy periods
of stress, worry, demoralization and frustration, all of which can result in
general health issues. While we question the value of the letter remaining on
file, some four years after the events in question, nothing in that letter
leads us to conclude that Dr. Gardener was guilty of pre‑litigation
misconduct.

[
148
]

We
are puzzled by the suggestion that the parties were not given an opportunity to
make submissions as to costs, as the trial judge requested and received written
submissions from all

parties. There is no indication
that counsel asked the trial judge to permit further submissions as to costs.
We have carefully considered the trial judge’s criticism of the unnecessarily
long trial, the lack of admissions, and detailed evidence relating to workplace
conflicts. However, we believe that the criticism was addressed not to the
appellant alone, but to all parties.

[
149
]

An
award of costs is a matter within the discretion of the trial judge, and
nothing in the submissions has persuaded us to set aside the trial judge’s
costs award.

[
150
]

The
appeal is dismissed.
